top_risks.title: Rule allows any source to reach any destination on any port
Firmware has a vulnerability that attackers are known to use
Firewall management is reachable from the internet
Rule never takes effect because an earlier rule does the opposite
Rule allows any source to reach any destination on any port
Traffic is allowed without any security inspection
Internet traffic can reach internal services too broadly
Admin accounts that can log in from anywhere

remediation.title: Rule allows any source to reach any destination on any port
remediation.recommendation: Replace it with rules for the sources, destinations and services people actually need. If it was added as a temporary fix, remove it.

remediation.title: Firmware has a vulnerability that attackers are known to use
remediation.recommendation: Upgrade to a fixed release as soon as you can. Until then, turn off or restrict the affected feature and check the firewall for signs of compromise as the advisory describes.

remediation.title: Firewall management is reachable from the internet
remediation.recommendation: Remove https, http, ssh, telnet and snmp from allowaccess on internet-facing interfaces. If you have to manage over the internet, limit sources with a local-in policy or use a VPN.

remediation.title: Rule never takes effect because an earlier rule does the opposite
remediation.recommendation: Move this rule above the broader one, or narrow the broader rule so it no longer covers this traffic.

remediation.title: Traffic is allowed without any security inspection
remediation.recommendation: Attach security profiles to the rule, at least IPS and antivirus, and make sure utm-status is enabled.

remediation.title: Internet traffic can reach internal services too broadly
remediation.recommendation: Publish only what must be public, through VIPs. Restrict sources where you can and put IPS on the rule. Admin protocols such as RDP and SSH belong behind a VPN.

remediation.title: Admin accounts without two-factor authentication
remediation.recommendation: Enable two-factor authentication (FortiToken, email or SMS) for every admin, or enforce MFA on the RADIUS or LDAP server that authenticates them.

remediation.title: Admin accounts that can log in from anywhere
remediation.recommendation: Set trusthost entries to your management networks. Trusted hosts only help if every admin account has them, and they don't stop attacks that happen before login, so also restrict the admin interfaces with a local-in policy.

remediation.title: Unencrypted admin access (HTTP or Telnet)
remediation.recommendation: Remove telnet and http from allowaccess on every interface and use SSH and HTTPS only.

remediation.title: Strong cryptography is turned off
remediation.recommendation: Turn it back on: config system global / set strong-crypto enable.

remediation.title: Service reachable from the internet without any inspection
remediation.recommendation: Add IPS to the rule (and antivirus where files are exchanged), use deep inspection if the service uses TLS and you can load its certificate, and limit sources where you can.

remediation.title: SSL-VPN portal open to the internet
remediation.recommendation: Keep the firmware on a fixed release, require MFA, restrict source addresses or countries, and consider moving users to IPsec VPN or ZTNA.

remediation.title: Scanners can't see inside encrypted traffic
remediation.recommendation: Use a deep-inspection SSL/SSH profile on rules where you rely on these scanners, with exemptions for sensitive categories such as banking and health.

remediation.title: Traffic between interfaces in a zone isn't filtered
remediation.recommendation: Set intrazone deny and write rules for the traffic that should flow, or split unrelated networks into separate zones.

remediation.title: Traffic logging is turned off on an allow rule
remediation.recommendation: Set logtraffic to all, or at least utm.

remediation.title: Weak password rules for admins
remediation.recommendation: Enable the admin password policy with a minimum length of 12 and at least two character types (config system password-policy).

remediation.title: Several accounts with full super_admin rights
remediation.recommendation: Keep super_admin to one or two accounts and give everyone else a profile limited to their job.

remediation.title: Logs aren't sent off the firewall
remediation.recommendation: Send logs to FortiAnalyzer, FortiAnalyzer Cloud or a syslog/SIEM server.

remediation.title: Deep inspection uses the built-in Fortinet CA
remediation.recommendation: Issue a subordinate CA from your own PKI for SSL inspection and push it to clients.

remediation.title: IPS sensor only watches, never blocks
remediation.recommendation: Set the action to block for high and critical signatures once you've checked for false positives.

remediation.title: Default 'admin' account still exists
remediation.recommendation: Create personal admin accounts, then rename or delete the default 'admin' account.

remediation.title: Admin sessions stay open too long
remediation.recommendation: Set admintimeout to a short value, such as 5 to 10 minutes.

remediation.title: Short lockout after failed admin logins
remediation.recommendation: Set admin-lockout-threshold to 3 and admin-lockout-duration to 900 seconds or more.

remediation.title: SSL-VPN uses the factory certificate
remediation.recommendation: Install a certificate from a trusted CA for the portal's hostname and set it as servercert.

remediation.title: Duplicate rule
remediation.recommendation: Delete the later copy.

remediation.title: Empty address or service group
remediation.recommendation: Add the intended members, or remove the group and the rules that use it.

remediation.title: Several address objects for the same network
remediation.recommendation: Keep one object per network and point all rules at it.

remediation.title: No external threat feeds
remediation.recommendation: If you have a feed you trust, add it under system external-resource and use it in rules or DNS filtering.

remediation.title: Address objects that overlap
remediation.recommendation: Check the pair and remove whichever one is left over, if any.

remediation.title: Local administrator accounts
remediation.recommendation: Authenticate admins against RADIUS, TACACS+ or LDAP with MFA. Keep a single local break-glass account with a long password stored offline.

remediation.title: Disabled rules left in the policy table
remediation.recommendation: Delete disabled rules you no longer need. If you keep one on purpose, say why in its comment.

remediation.title: Rules without a comment
remediation.recommendation: Add a comment with the purpose and the ticket or change number.

remediation.title: Check this firmware version against Fortinet advisories
remediation.recommendation: Look this model and version up on the Fortinet PSIRT site and upgrade to a fixed release if anything applies.

remediation.title: No login banner
remediation.recommendation: Enable pre-login-banner in system global and set the text under config system replacemsg admin.

remediation.title: No high availability
remediation.recommendation: If this firewall carries production traffic, consider an HA pair.

remediation.title: Unused address objects
remediation.recommendation: Delete them after checking that nothing outside this firewall (FortiManager, scripts) depends on them.

remediation.title: Unused custom services
remediation.recommendation: Delete custom services you no longer need.

findings.title: Rule allows any source to reach any destination on any port
findings.description: Policy 3 "WAN-Full-Access" allows any source to reach any destination on any service, for traffic coming in from the internet.
findings.impact: Anything that arrives on the rule's interfaces gets through. Segmentation stops at this rule, and an attacker who lands on one side can reach everything on the other.
findings.recommendation: Replace it with rules for the sources, destinations and services people actually need. If it was added as a temporary fix, remove it.
evidence: wan1 -> dmz; from any IPv4 address to any IPv4 address; service ALL; action accept

findings.title: Firmware has a vulnerability that attackers are known to use
findings.description: FortiOS 7.2.5 is affected by CVE-2024-21762 (FG-IR-24-015): an out-of-bounds write in the SSL-VPN daemon that lets an unauthenticated attacker run code on the firewall. The vulnerable code is in SSL-VPN, which is enabled on wan1 here and reachable from the internet. It's in CISA's catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities.
findings.impact: This version is in the affected range of a vulnerability that has been exploited in real attacks, and the feature it lives in is in use here.
findings.recommendation: Upgrade to a fixed release as soon as you can. Until then, turn off or restrict the affected feature and check the firewall for signs of compromise as the advisory describes.
evidence: Source: built-in advisory list; confirm on the Fortinet PSIRT site

findings.title: Firewall management is reachable from the internet
findings.description: Interface wan1 faces the internet (it has role wan) and accepts HTTPS, HTTP, SSH and telnet management connections from any address.
findings.impact: The admin login page, SSH or SNMP is open on an internet-facing interface. FortiOS has had several authentication bypass bugs in the admin interface, and exposed management is scanned constantly.
findings.recommendation: Remove https, http, ssh, telnet and snmp from allowaccess on internet-facing interfaces. If you have to manage over the internet, limit sources with a local-in policy or use a VPN.
evidence: allowaccess ping https ssh telnet http

findings.title: Rule never takes effect because an earlier rule does the opposite
findings.description: Policy 5 "Deny-Partner-SSH-shadowed" (deny) sits below policy 4 "Allow-Partner-SSH" (accept), and policy 4 already matches every packet policy 5 would. FortiGate uses the first match, so policy 5 never takes effect and the traffic it's meant to block is allowed.
findings.impact: FortiGate stops at the first matching rule. An earlier rule with the opposite action catches all of this rule's traffic, so a block here doesn't block anything, or an allow here never allows anything.
findings.recommendation: Move this rule above the broader one, or narrow the broader rule so it no longer covers this traffic.
evidence: never reached: internal -> dmz; from 198.51.100.0/24 to 10.0.0.50/32; service tcp/22; action deny
matched first: internal -> dmz; from 198.51.100.0/24 to 10.0.0.0/24; service tcp/22; action accept

findings.title: Rule allows any source to reach any destination on any port
findings.description: Policy 2 "Outbound-Any" allows any source to reach any destination on any service, for traffic going out to the internet.
findings.impact: Anything that arrives on the rule's interfaces gets through. Segmentation stops at this rule, and an attacker who lands on one side can reach everything on the other.
findings.recommendation: Replace it with rules for the sources, destinations and services people actually need. If it was added as a temporary fix, remove it.
evidence: internal -> wan1; from any IPv4 address to any IPv4 address; service ALL; action accept

findings.title: Traffic is allowed without any security inspection
findings.description: Policy 2 "Outbound-Any" allows traffic going out to the internet without any security profile.
findings.impact: No IPS, antivirus, web, DNS or application control looks at this traffic, so malware and exploit attempts pass straight through.
findings.recommendation: Attach security profiles to the rule, at least IPS and antivirus, and make sure utm-status is enabled.
evidence: internal -> wan1; from any IPv4 address to any IPv4 address; service ALL; action accept

findings.title: Internet traffic can reach internal services too broadly
findings.description: Policy 3 "WAN-Full-Access" lets internet traffic reach every service.
findings.impact: A rule from an internet-facing interface opens more than a single published service, or opens remote-access protocols that attackers scan for all day.
findings.recommendation: Publish only what must be public, through VIPs. Restrict sources where you can and put IPS on the rule. Admin protocols such as RDP and SSH belong behind a VPN.
evidence: wan1 -> dmz; from any IPv4 address to any IPv4 address; service ALL; action accept

findings.title: Admin accounts without two-factor authentication
findings.description: 3 admin accounts can log in with a password alone: admin, backup_admin, thirdsuper.
findings.impact: A stolen or guessed password is enough to take over the firewall.
findings.recommendation: Enable two-factor authentication (FortiToken, email or SMS) for every admin, or enforce MFA on the RADIUS or LDAP server that authenticates them.

findings.title: Admin accounts that can log in from anywhere
findings.description: 2 admin accounts have no trusted hosts and can log in from any address that reaches the admin interface: admin, backup_admin. Because not every account is restricted, trusted hosts don't limit who can reach the login page at all.
findings.impact: Without trusted hosts, anyone who can reach the admin interface can try these accounts' passwords.
findings.recommendation: Set trusthost entries to your management networks. Trusted hosts only help if every admin account has them, and they don't stop attacks that happen before login, so also restrict the admin interfaces with a local-in policy.

findings.title: Unencrypted admin access (HTTP or Telnet)
findings.description: Telnet, which sends passwords in clear text, is enabled on wan1. HTTP admin access is enabled on wan1. It only redirects to HTTPS, but that first request can be intercepted.
findings.impact: Telnet sends passwords in clear text. HTTP only redirects to HTTPS, but someone on the path can intercept that redirect.
findings.recommendation: Remove telnet and http from allowaccess on every interface and use SSH and HTTPS only.
evidence: config system interface / edit wan1 (allowaccess includes telnet)
config system interface / edit wan1 (allowaccess includes http)

findings.title: Strong cryptography is turned off
findings.description: Strong-crypto is disabled, so the firewall's own HTTPS, SSH and FortiGuard connections may use weak ciphers.
findings.impact: The firewall will accept weak ciphers and old protocols for its own HTTPS, SSH and FortiGuard connections.
findings.recommendation: Turn it back on: config system global / set strong-crypto enable.

findings.title: Service reachable from the internet without any inspection
findings.description: VIP WEB_VIP publishes 203.0.113.10:443/tcp to 10.0.0.50:443, and policy 1 "Inbound-Web-VIP" lets the internet reach it (tcp/443). The rule has no security profile, so nothing inspects that traffic.
findings.impact: A server is reachable from the internet and the rule that lets traffic in has no security profile. Exploit attempts reach it untouched, and published servers are among the first things attackers probe.
findings.recommendation: Add IPS to the rule (and antivirus where files are exchanged), use deep inspection if the service uses TLS and you can load its certificate, and limit sources where you can.

findings.title: Service reachable from the internet without any inspection
findings.description: Policy 3 "WAN-Full-Access" lets internet traffic from any IPv4 address reach any IPv4 address on any port. The rule has no security profile, so nothing inspects that traffic.
findings.impact: A server is reachable from the internet and the rule that lets traffic in has no security profile. Exploit attempts reach it untouched, and published servers are among the first things attackers probe.
findings.recommendation: Add IPS to the rule (and antivirus where files are exchanged), use deep inspection if the service uses TLS and you can load its certificate, and limit sources where you can.

findings.title: SSL-VPN portal open to the internet
findings.description: SSL-VPN is enabled on wan1, which faces the internet, and the firewall runs FortiOS 7.2.5. Any source address can reach the login page. Web mode is on in portal full-access, which puts more code within reach of the internet.
findings.impact: The FortiGate SSL-VPN has had several critical bugs that let attackers in before login, and they have been exploited at scale. An internet-facing portal needs current firmware and tight controls.
findings.recommendation: Keep the firmware on a fixed release, require MFA, restrict source addresses or countries, and consider moving users to IPsec VPN or ZTNA.

findings.title: Scanners can't see inside encrypted traffic
findings.description: Policy 4 "Allow-Partner-SSH" relies on IPS and antivirus, but its SSL profile (cert-inspect) only does certificate inspection. Encrypted content passes these scanners unseen.
findings.impact: Antivirus, DLP, file filtering and email filtering need decrypted content. With certificate inspection or no inspection they only see the handshake, so most modern traffic goes unscanned.
findings.recommendation: Use a deep-inspection SSL/SSH profile on rules where you rely on these scanners, with exemptions for sensitive categories such as banking and health.
evidence: internal -> dmz; from 198.51.100.0/24 to 10.0.0.0/24; service tcp/22; action accept

findings.title: Traffic between interfaces in a zone isn't filtered
findings.description: Zone 'DMZ_ZONE' has intrazone set to allow, so traffic between its 2 interfaces (dmz, internal) passes without any rule. The policy table won't show it.
findings.impact: With intrazone allow, traffic between the zone's interfaces passes without any rule. If they are different segments there's no segmentation between them, and it won't show up in the policy table.
findings.recommendation: Set intrazone deny and write rules for the traffic that should flow, or split unrelated networks into separate zones.

findings.title: Traffic logging is turned off on an allow rule
findings.description: Policy 2 "Outbound-Any" allows traffic going out to the internet with logging turned off.
findings.impact: Sessions this rule allows leave no record, so there's nothing to look at after an incident.
findings.recommendation: Set logtraffic to all, or at least utm.
evidence: internal -> wan1; from any IPv4 address to any IPv4 address; service ALL; action accept

findings.title: Weak password rules for admins
findings.description: The admin password policy is turned off, so any password is accepted.
findings.impact: Without length and complexity rules, admins can set short passwords that are quick to guess.
findings.recommendation: Enable the admin password policy with a minimum length of 12 and at least two character types (config system password-policy).

findings.title: Several accounts with full super_admin rights
findings.description: 3 accounts have the super_admin profile: admin, backup_admin, thirdsuper.
findings.impact: Each super_admin account can change anything. The more of them there are, the more ways in, and the harder it is to tell who changed what.
findings.recommendation: Keep super_admin to one or two accounts and give everyone else a profile limited to their job.

findings.title: Rule allows any source to reach any destination on any port
findings.description: Policy 9 "DMZ-Intrazone-Traffic" allows any source to reach any destination on any service, for traffic inside one zone.
findings.impact: Anything that arrives on the rule's interfaces gets through. Segmentation stops at this rule, and an attacker who lands on one side can reach everything on the other.
findings.recommendation: Replace it with rules for the sources, destinations and services people actually need. If it was added as a temporary fix, remove it.
evidence: dmz, internal -> dmz, internal; from any IPv4 address to any IPv4 address; service ALL; action accept

findings.title: Traffic is allowed without any security inspection
findings.description: Policy 9 "DMZ-Intrazone-Traffic" allows traffic inside one zone without any security profile.
findings.impact: No IPS, antivirus, web, DNS or application control looks at this traffic, so malware and exploit attempts pass straight through.
findings.recommendation: Attach security profiles to the rule, at least IPS and antivirus, and make sure utm-status is enabled.
evidence: dmz, internal -> dmz, internal; from any IPv4 address to any IPv4 address; service ALL; action accept

findings.title: Logs aren't sent off the firewall
findings.description: No remote log destination is enabled: no FortiAnalyzer, no FortiCloud logging and no syslog server. Logs exist only on the firewall itself.
findings.impact: Logs stay on the device, where space is limited and anyone who takes over the firewall can delete them.
findings.recommendation: Send logs to FortiAnalyzer, FortiAnalyzer Cloud or a syslog/SIEM server.
evidence: no log fortianalyzer or log syslogd settings are enabled

findings.title: Deep inspection uses the built-in Fortinet CA
findings.description: SSL/SSH profile 'deep-default-ca' does deep inspection and signs with the factory CA 'Fortinet_CA_SSL'.
findings.impact: Clients have to trust the CA that deep inspection signs with. The factory Fortinet CA isn't part of your PKI and isn't managed by you, which weakens the whole setup.
findings.recommendation: Issue a subordinate CA from your own PKI for SSL inspection and push it to clients.

findings.title: IPS sensor only watches, never blocks
findings.description: IPS sensor 'ips-monitor' is used by rules, but every signature action in it is monitor or pass. Nothing gets blocked.
findings.impact: Every configured signature action is monitor or pass. Attacks get logged but still reach their target.
findings.recommendation: Set the action to block for high and critical signatures once you've checked for false positives.

findings.title: Default 'admin' account still exists
findings.description: The factory account name 'admin' is still in use.
findings.impact: 'admin' is the first username every attacker tries, so keeping it gives away half of the login.
findings.recommendation: Create personal admin accounts, then rename or delete the default 'admin' account.

findings.title: Firmware has a vulnerability that attackers are known to use
findings.description: FortiOS 7.2.5 is affected by CVE-2024-23113 (FG-IR-24-029): a format string bug in the FortiManager connection daemon (fgfm) that can be exploited without logging in. The vulnerable code is in FortiManager access (fgfm), which isn't enabled in this backup, so it can't be reached right now. Upgrade anyway: one config change would expose it.
findings.impact: This version is in the affected range of a vulnerability that has been exploited in real attacks, and the feature it lives in is in use here.
findings.recommendation: Upgrade to a fixed release as soon as you can. Until then, turn off or restrict the affected feature and check the firewall for signs of compromise as the advisory describes.
evidence: FortiManager access (fgfm): no interface allows fgfm access
Source: built-in advisory list; confirm on the Fortinet PSIRT site

findings.title: Admin sessions stay open too long
findings.description: Idle admin sessions time out after 480 minutes. The review's limit is 15 minutes.
findings.impact: An unattended logged-in session can be used by whoever sits down at it or manages to hijack it.
findings.recommendation: Set admintimeout to a short value, such as 5 to 10 minutes.

findings.title: Short lockout after failed admin logins
findings.description: Admin login lockout is weak: the lockout only lasts 60 seconds.
findings.impact: After a few wrong passwords the admin login is only blocked briefly, so password guessing can carry on at a steady pace.
findings.recommendation: Set admin-lockout-threshold to 3 and admin-lockout-duration to 900 seconds or more.

findings.title: SSL-VPN uses the factory certificate
findings.description: The SSL-VPN portal presents the factory certificate 'Fortinet_Factory'.
findings.impact: Users see a certificate warning every time they connect and learn to click through it. That makes a fake portal much easier to pass off.
findings.recommendation: Install a certificate from a trusted CA for the portal's hostname and set it as servercert.

findings.title: Duplicate rule
findings.description: Policy 7 "Redundant-Web-B" is an exact copy of policy 6 "Redundant-Web-A": same traffic, same action, same NAT, inspection and logging. Policy 7 never gets used.
findings.impact: Two rules match exactly the same traffic and treat it the same way. The second one never does anything.
findings.recommendation: Delete the later copy.
evidence: internal -> dmz; from 192.168.1.0/24 to 10.0.0.50/32; service tcp/443; action accept

findings.title: Empty address or service group
findings.description: Address group 'EMPTY_GROUP' has no members.
findings.impact: A group without members usually matches nothing, which quietly disables any rule that uses it. That's almost always a mistake.
findings.recommendation: Add the intended members, or remove the group and the rules that use it.

findings.title: Several address objects for the same network
findings.description: 2 address objects all define 10.0.0.50/32: WEB_SERVER, WEB_SERVER_DUP.
findings.impact: When one network has several names, rules drift apart as people update one object and not the others.
findings.recommendation: Keep one object per network and point all rules at it.

findings.title: Traffic is allowed without any security inspection
findings.description: 2 rules allow narrow internal traffic without any security profile: 6, 7. Each one is low risk on its own, but together they show how much east-west traffic goes uninspected.
findings.impact: No IPS, antivirus, web, DNS or application control looks at this traffic, so malware and exploit attempts pass straight through.
findings.recommendation: Attach security profiles to the rule, at least IPS and antivirus, and make sure utm-status is enabled.

findings.title: No external threat feeds
findings.description: No external threat feeds are configured.
findings.impact: Threat feeds let rules block known-bad addresses and domains automatically. Not having one is a missed opportunity rather than a hole.
findings.recommendation: If you have a feed you trust, add it under system external-resource and use it in rules or DNS filtering.
evidence: config system external-resource has no entries

findings.title: Local administrator accounts
findings.description: 3 admin accounts are local to the firewall rather than checked against a central directory: admin, backup_admin, thirdsuper.
findings.impact: Local accounts live only on this firewall. Your central password, MFA and offboarding processes don't reach them, so old accounts tend to linger.
findings.recommendation: Authenticate admins against RADIUS, TACACS+ or LDAP with MFA. Keep a single local break-glass account with a long password stored offline.

findings.title: Disabled rules left in the policy table
findings.description: Rule 8 is disabled but still in the table.
findings.impact: Old disabled rules slow down reviews and can be switched back on by accident.
findings.recommendation: Delete disabled rules you no longer need. If you keep one on purpose, say why in its comment.

findings.title: Rules without a comment
findings.description: 8 rules have no comment: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9.
findings.impact: Without a comment nobody can tell later why a rule exists or who asked for it.
findings.recommendation: Add a comment with the purpose and the ticket or change number.

findings.title: Check this firmware version against Fortinet advisories
findings.description: The backup is from an FGVM64 running FortiOS 7.2.5 (build 1517). Check it against the current Fortinet PSIRT advisories; this review only knows about issues up to its own release.
findings.impact: Which vulnerabilities apply depends on the exact firmware. An offline review can't know about advisories published after it was written.
findings.recommendation: Look this model and version up on the Fortinet PSIRT site and upgrade to a fixed release if anything applies.

findings.title: No login banner
findings.description: No banner is shown before admin login.
findings.impact: A banner tells people that access is monitored and only for authorised users. Some regulations and internal policies require one.
findings.recommendation: Enable pre-login-banner in system global and set the text under config system replacemsg admin.

findings.title: No high availability
findings.description: This firewall runs on its own, without an HA partner.
findings.impact: If this unit fails, traffic stops until it's replaced. That can be a sensible choice for a small site.
findings.recommendation: If this firewall carries production traffic, consider an HA pair.
evidence: config system ha is at its defaults

findings.title: Unused address objects
findings.description: 2 address objects in VDOM root are not referenced anywhere this review looks (rules, groups, routes, VPN and SD-WAN settings): UNUSED_HOST, WEB_SERVER_DUP.
findings.impact: Objects that nothing references clutter the configuration and are easy to reuse by mistake.
findings.recommendation: Delete them after checking that nothing outside this firewall (FortiManager, scripts) depends on them.

findings.title: Unused custom services
findings.description: 1 custom service in VDOM root is not referenced anywhere this review looks (rules, groups, routes, VPN and SD-WAN settings): TCP_8080.
findings.impact: Custom services that nothing references are clutter.
findings.recommendation: Delete custom services you no longer need.
evidence: config firewall service custom / edit TCP_8080 (line 78)

findings.title: Address objects that overlap
findings.description: 'WEB_SERVER' (10.0.0.50/32) sits inside 'DMZ_NET' (10.0.0.0/24).
findings.impact: One network sits inside another under a different name. That's often fine, but it can hide conflicting intent.
findings.recommendation: Check the pair and remove whichever one is left over, if any.

findings.title: Address objects that overlap
findings.description: 'WEB_SERVER_DUP' (10.0.0.50/32) sits inside 'DMZ_NET' (10.0.0.0/24).
findings.impact: One network sits inside another under a different name. That's often fine, but it can hide conflicting intent.
findings.recommendation: Check the pair and remove whichever one is left over, if any.
